claim: Alzheimer's disease currently affects more than 1 in 9 people above 65 years of age (11.2%) in the USA.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) currently affects >1 in 9 people above 65 years of age (11.2%) in the USA and is the seventh cause of death worldwide (Alzheimer's Association, 2022; Mortality and global health estimates, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to external sources (Alzheimer's Association, 2022; Mortality and global health estimates, 2019).

claim: Alzheimer's disease is the seventh cause of death worldwide.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) currently affects >1 in 9 people above 65 years of age (11.2%) in the USA and is the seventh cause of death worldwide (Alzheimer's Association, 2022; Mortality and global health estimates, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to external sources (Alzheimer's Association, 2022; Mortality and global health estimates, 2019).

claim: A hallmark of Alzheimer's disease is the extracellular aggregation of amyloid beta (Aβ).
source: A hallmark of AD is the extracellular aggregation of amyloid beta (Aβ).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of Alzheimer's research, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Non-enzymatic pathways for clearing Aβ from the brain include the continuous flow of the interstitial fluid into the cerebrospinal fluid followed by interstitial fluid drainage.
source: The non-enzymatic pathways include the continuous flow of the interstitial fluid into the cerebrospinal fluid followed by interstitial fluid drainage, phagocytosis by microglia or astrocytes, and receptor-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: Non-enzymatic pathways for clearing Aβ from the brain include phagocytosis by microglia or astrocytes.
source: The non-enzymatic pathways include the continuous flow of the interstitial fluid into the cerebrospinal fluid followed by interstitial fluid drainage, phagocytosis by microglia or astrocytes, and receptor-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: Non-enzymatic pathways for clearing Aβ from the brain include receptor-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier.
source: The non-enzymatic pathways include the continuous flow of the interstitial fluid into the cerebrospinal fluid followed by interstitial fluid drainage, phagocytosis by microglia or astrocytes, and receptor-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Elbert et al., 2022; Sagare et al., 2007; Tajbakhsh et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2015).

claim: The enzymatic pathway for clearing Aβ involves several proteases, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMP), neprilysin, insulin-degrading enzymes, and glutamate carboxypeptidase.
source: The enzymatic pathway involves several proteases, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMP), neprilysin, insulin-degrading enzymes, and glutamate carboxypeptidase (Nalivaeva et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Nalivaeva et al., 2012).

claim: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) can block the clearance of Aβ.
source: The extracellular protein heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) can block the clearance of Aβ.
evidence: This is stated as a general fact in the introduction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: HSPGs are often found in Aβ depositions where they might block enzymatic degradation.
source: HSPGs are often found in Aβ depositions where they might block enzymatic degradation (Gupta-Bansal et al., 1995; Su et al., 1992; van Horssen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Gupta-Bansal et al., 1995; Su et al., 1992; van Horssen et al., 2002).

claim: Most HSPGs promote the uptake of Aβ through lipid rafts.
source: Moreover, while most HSPGs promote the uptake of Aβ through lipid rafts, uptake of Aβ through clathrin-mediated endocytosis is blocked when the HSPG (SDC3) binds to Aβ (Letoha et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Letoha et al., 2019).

claim: Uptake of Aβ through clathrin-mediated endocytosis is blocked when the HSPG (SDC3) binds to Aβ.
source: Moreover, while most HSPGs promote the uptake of Aβ through lipid rafts, uptake of Aβ through clathrin-mediated endocytosis is blocked when the HSPG (SDC3) binds to Aβ (Letoha et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Letoha et al., 2019).

claim: Specific collagens consistently co-aggregate with Aβ plaques.
source: One of the least understood observations is the consistent co-aggregation of specific collagens with Aβ plaques.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: The compaction of Aβ into plaques can be influenced by the expression of collagenous amyloid plaque components (CLACs).
source: Interestingly, the compaction of Aβ into plaques can be influenced by the expression of collagenous amyloid plaque components (CLACs) (Hashimoto et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Hashimoto et al., 2020).

claim: CLAC is a collagen type XXV a1 chain (COL25A1) cleavage product.
source: CLAC is a collagen type XXV a1 chain (COL25A1) cleavage product.
evidence: This is stated as a fact, representing established knowledge.

claim: COL25A1 overexpression can have detrimental effects in mice.
source: COL25A1 overexpression can have detrimental effects in mice (Tong et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Tong et al., 2010).

claim: Certain single nucleotide polymorphisms in COL25A1 are associated with Alzheimer's disease.
source: However, human genetic studies suggest a more complex interplay where certain single nucleotide polymorphisms in COL25A1 are associated with AD and others are, in contrast, associated with health effects in the elderly (Erikson et al., 2016; Forsell et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Erikson et al., 2016; Forsell et al., 2010).

claim: Certain single nucleotide polymorphisms in COL25A1 are associated with health effects in the elderly.
source: However, human genetic studies suggest a more complex interplay where certain single nucleotide polymorphisms in COL25A1 are associated with AD and others are, in contrast, associated with health effects in the elderly (Erikson et al., 2016; Forsell et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Erikson et al., 2016; Forsell et al., 2010).

claim: Collagen XVIII colocalizes with vascular amyloid at the basal lamina and reduces disease symptoms.
source: Colocalizing with vascular amyloid at the basal lamina is collagen XVIII, an HSPG that reduces disease symptoms (van Horssen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (van Horssen et al., 2002).

claim: Collagen VI can block the interaction between neurons and oligomers and help protect against neurotoxicity.
source: Collagen VI was found at the extracellular matrix (ECM) and the basal lamina and can block the interaction between neurons and oligomers and help protect against neurotoxicity (Cheng et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Cheng et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2020).

claim: The basement lamina collagen IV was 55% upregulated in cerebral vessels when comparing AD to healthy subjects.
source: Furthermore, the basement lamina collagen IV was 55% upregulated in cerebral vessels when comparing AD to healthy subjects (Cheng et al., 2009; Farkas et al., 2000; Kalaria and Pax, 1995; Nguyen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Cheng et al., 2009; Farkas et al., 2000; Kalaria and Pax, 1995; Nguyen et al., 2021).

claim: A positive correlation was reported between disease progression (Braak stage) and collagen IV deposition.
source: A positive correlation was reported between disease progression (Braak stage) and collagen IV deposition.
evidence: This is stated as a reported finding, representing established knowledge from the literature.

claim: An increase in collagen IV deposition was found per mm2 gray matter with each group: control (Braak stage <2), preclinical (Braak stage >2, <4), and AD patients (Braak stage >4).
source: With each group: control (Braak stage <2), preclinical (Braak stage >2, <4), and AD patients (Braak stage >4), an increase in collagen IV deposition was found per mm2 gray matter (Lepelletier et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Lepelletier et al., 2017).

claim: Collagen IV was shown to bind the amyloid precursor protein (APP).
source: Collagen IV was shown to bind the amyloid precursor protein (APP), prevent Aβ fibril formation, and even disrupt preformed Aβ fibrils (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).

claim: Collagen IV can prevent Aβ fibril formation.
source: Collagen IV was shown to bind the amyloid precursor protein (APP), prevent Aβ fibril formation, and even disrupt preformed Aβ fibrils (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).

claim: Collagen IV can disrupt preformed Aβ fibrils.
source: Collagen IV was shown to bind the amyloid precursor protein (APP), prevent Aβ fibril formation, and even disrupt preformed Aβ fibrils (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Kiuchi et al., 2002a; Kiuchi et al., 2002b ; Narindrasorasak et al., 1995).

claim: Several Alzheimer-related pathways are highly conserved between humans and C. elegans.
source: Several Alzheimer-related pathways are highly conserved between humans and C. elegans (Apostolakou et al., 2021; Ewald and Li, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Apostolakou et al., 2021; Ewald and Li, 2010).

claim: The C. elegans EMB-9 and LET-2 are collagen type IV.
source: The C. elegans EMB-9 and LET-2 are collagen type IV, CLE-1 is collagen type XVIII, and COL-99 is collagen type XXV (Teuscher et al., 2019a).

claim: CLE-1 is collagen type XVIII in C. elegans.
source: The C. elegans EMB-9 and LET-2 are collagen type IV, CLE-1 is collagen type XVIII, and COL-99 is collagen type XXV (Teuscher et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Teuscher et al., 2019a).

claim: COL-99 is collagen type XXV in C. elegans.
source: The C. elegans EMB-9 and LET-2 are collagen type IV, CLE-1 is collagen type XVIII, and COL-99 is collagen type XXV (Teuscher et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Teuscher et al., 2019a).

claim: EMB-9 and LET-2 localize to the basal lamina in C. elegans.
source: While EMB-9 and LET-2 localize to the basal lamina, CLE-1 and COL-99 localize to neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about C. elegans biology, representing established knowledge.

claim: CLE-1 and COL-99 localize to neurons in C. elegans.
source: While EMB-9 and LET-2 localize to the basal lamina, CLE-1 and COL-99 localize to neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about C. elegans biology, representing established knowledge.

claim: Upon induction, secreted sfGFP::Aβ is initially cleared by the excretory system, the gut, and the coelomocytes.
source: Here, we show that upon induction, secreted sfGFP::Aβ is initially cleared by the excretory system, the gut, and the coelomocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aβ is retained past 24 hr and forms non-mobile structures in the ECM.
source: However, Aβ is retained past 24 hr and forms non-mobile structures in the ECM.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Collagens can completely suppress Aβ aggregate formation.
source: We identified collagens that can completely suppress Aβ aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Metalloproteases assist in the removal of extracellular Aβ aggregates.
source: Moreover, we find modulators of the ECM, metalloproteases, to assist in the removal of extracellular Aβ aggregates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ADM-2 is essential to remove Aβ aggregates.
source: We demonstrate that one of these metalloproteases, a disintegrin and metalloprotease 2 (ADM-2), is essential to remove Aβ aggregates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previous human Aβ expressing C. elegans strains failed to secrete Aβ and model intracellular Aβ toxicity.
source: Previous human Aβ expressing C. elegans strains failed to secrete Aβ and model intracellular Aβ toxicity (Ewald and Li, 2012; Link, 1995).

claim: The hsp-16.2 promoter drives expression predominantly in neurons and hypodermis.
source: Expression of this construct was induced by heat shock under the control of the hsp-16.2 promoter that drives expression in many tissues but predominantly in neurons and hypodermis (Bacaj and Shaham, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Bacaj and Shaham, 2007).

claim: sfGFP is more stable in the extracellular space than classical GFP.
source: We used sfGFP because it is more stable in the extracellular space than classical GFP (Pédelacq et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Pédelacq et al., 2006).

claim: The full length of the Aβ1-42 peptide is essential for its aggregation.
source: The full length of the Aβ1-42 peptide is essential for its aggregation (McColl et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (McColl et al., 2012).

claim: After a single heat-shock induction of sfGFP::Aβ, sfGFP::Aβ was expressed in many tissues and secreted into the extracellular space surrounding different tissues.
source: After a single heat-shock induction of sfGFP::Aβ (i.e., single pulse-chase), sfGFP::Aβ was expressed in many tissues and secreted into the extracellular space surrounding different tissues (Figure 1C).

claim: Initially, Aβ localized to neurons in the nerve ring, the gut, the canal cells, the excretory canal, the canal-associated neurons, and the uterus.
source: Initially, Aβ localized to neurons in the nerve ring, the gut, the canal cells, the excretory canal, the canal-associated neurons, and the uterus (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figures 1C and D.

claim: During the first 24 hr, most of the sfGFP::Aβ appeared diffuse.
source: During the first 24 hr, most of the sfGFP::Aβ appeared diffuse.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After 24 hr, bright puncta were observed localized to the pharyngeal cuticle, the coelomocytes, and the cuticle.
source: After 24 hr, we observed bright puncta localized to the pharyngeal cuticle, the coelomocytes, and the cuticle (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 1D.

claim: sfGFP::Aβ fluorescent puncta remained for up to 8 days after induction at the cuticle, coelomocytes, and the uterus.
source: Remarkably, these sfGFP::Aβ fluorescent puncta remained for an exceptionally long time at the cuticle, coelomocytes, and the uterus, up to 8 days after induction (Figure 1D).

claim: Western blotting using GFP or Aβ antibodies confirmed that sfGFP::Aβ fluorescent puncta contain the human Aβ.
source: By western blotting using GFP or Aβ antibodies, we confirmed that these sfGFP::Aβ fluorescent puncta contain the human Aβ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After heat shock, all three strains (sfGFP::Aβ, sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P), and sfGFP-only) showed similar time course trajectories for the induction.
source: After heat shock, all three strains showed similar time course trajectories for the induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At the 24 hr time point, the non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P) and the sfGFP-only strains almost completely lost the GFP signal.
source: However, at the 24 hr time point where the sfGFP::Aβ was observed at the cuticle, the non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P), and the sfGFP-only strains almost completely lost the GFP signal (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figures 1E and 1—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: No localization to the cuticle was observed at the 24 hr time point for non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P) and sfGFP-only strains.
source: No localization to the cuticle was observed at this time point.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The retention at the cuticle after 24 hr was specific to Aβ1-42 due to its ability to form aggregates.
source: At the same time, the retention at the cuticle after 24 hr was specific to Aβ1-42 due to its ability to form aggregates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing aggregating and non-aggregating forms of Aβ.

claim: At 16 hr post-induction, the non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P) formed a striped pattern, equally distributed along the body, reminiscent of the striped pattern of furrows on the cuticle.
source: At 16 hr post-induction, the non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P) formed a striped pattern, equally distributed along the body, reminiscent of the striped pattern of furrows on the cuticle.

claim: sfGFP::Aβ formed two types of bright structures, named 'flower' and 'moss'.
source: By contrast, sfGFP::Aβ formed two types of bright structures, which we named 'flower' and 'moss' (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 2B.

claim: The 'flower' structures were exclusively found over the nematode's dorsal and ventral sides, where muscle tissue underlies the hypodermis.
source: Interestingly, the 'flower' structures were exclusively found over the nematode's dorsal and ventral sides, where muscle tissue underlies the hypodermis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 'moss' structures were consistently found on the left and right sides of the nematode, apical to the main hypodermal syncytium (hyp7).
source: The 'moss' structures were consistently found on the left and right sides of the nematode, apical to the main hypodermal syncytium (hyp7).

claim: The localization of the aggregate type is invariant and correlates with the underlying tissue type.
source: The localization of the aggregate type is invariant and correlates with the underlying tissue type.

source: The flower and moss structures are not found for the non-aggregating sfGFP::Aβ(F20S, L35P) (Figure 2A) nor for GFP-only (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) but were unique to the wild-type sfGFP::Aβ strain.

claim: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching showed both the moss and flower structures are immobile.

claim: Even when one-half of a single moss structure was photobleached, there was no recovery in the bleached area, indicating no movement or exchange of molecules even within the structure.
source: Even when one-half of a single moss structure was photobleached, there was no recovery in the bleached area, indicating no movement or exchange of molecules even within the structure (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 2C.

claim: Upon photobleaching, the flower structures turn completely dark.
source: Upon photobleaching, the flower structures turn completely dark (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data and Figure 2D.

claim: The surrounding, relatively low GFP intensity recovered rapidly (within seconds) after photobleaching of flower structures, but the flower structure remained dark.
source: The surrounding, relatively low GFP intensity recovered rapidly (within seconds), but the flower structure remained dark.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No recovery of signal inside the flower structure was observed for up to 4 hr.
source: No recovery of signal inside the structure was observed; however, after 4 hr, some bright dots were observed on the edge of the flower structures, indicating potential growth or exchange of Aβ from outside the photobleached area.

claim: After 4 hr, some bright dots were observed on the edge of the flower structures, indicating potential growth or exchange of Aβ from outside the photobleached area.

claim: The absence of fluorescence recovery for up to 4 hr confirmed that the flower and moss structures are immobile, suggesting that these structures are aggregates.

claim: The sfGFP::Aβ was observed to localize to two different parts of the cuticular ECM.

claim: The localization apical to the hypodermis, underneath the collagen-dense cuticle, is representative of the 'moss' type aggregates.

claim: The localization to the cortical layer of the cuticle is representative of the 'flower' type aggregates.

claim: 176 genes from 2368 screened genes were identified to increase or decrease sfGFP::Aβ intensity in vivo.

claim: 71 orthologs of AD implicated genes were identified in the screen.
source: Reassuringly, we identified 71 orthologs of AD implicated genes (category 2, Figure 3C, Supplementary file 2), suggesting the conservation of key molecular players relevant to human disease.

claim: The knockdown of MMP increased Aβ levels.

claim: The knockdown of several individual collagens either increased or decreased sfGFP::Aβ fluorescence.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Hales and Beattie, 1993) and experimental data.

claim: Treatment with collagen cross-linking inhibitor BAPN resulted in higher overall sfGFP::Aβ fluorescence.

claim: Collagen biogenesis and collagen stability can affect Aβ aggregate levels.

claim: Exposure to batimastat increased the sfGFP::Aβ load.

claim: When the inhibitor of metalloproteases is removed, the metalloproteases increase their activity and remove the sfGFP::Aβ.

claim: cri-2(gk314) mutants showed lower levels of sfGFP::Aβ compared to a wild-type background at the 24 hr time point.
